questions.question: What kernel architectural principles distinguish a Hard Real-Time Operating System (RTOS, like FreeRTOS or VxWorks) from a general-purpose OS running the PREEMPT_RT patch?

questions.question: What is the difference between Resident Set Size (RSS) and Virtual Memory Size (VSZ) when analyzing a process's memory footprint?

questions.question: What do the three Linux Memory Overcommit modes (0, 1, and 2 in /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory) configure?

questions.question: What are CPU frequency scaling governors (such as performance, powersave, and schedutil) in modern operating systems?

questions.question: What is Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT / Hyper-Threading), and how does the operating system view logical versus physical cores?

questions.question: Why is the rename() system call atomic in POSIX file systems, and how is it used to implement safe, crash-proof file updates?

questions.question: What is the core difference between Discretionary Access Control (DAC) and Mandatory Access Control (MAC) in operating system security?

questions.question: What is the difference between Paravirtualization and Full Virtualization?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: explains Full Virtualization: guest OS runs completely unmodified, unaware it is virtualized; hardware is fully emulated
explains Paravirtualization: guest OS kernel is modified to make explicit 'hypercalls' directly to the hypervisor

questions.question: What does the 'isolcpus' Linux kernel boot parameter do, and why do high-frequency trading and real-time systems use it?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

describes how dedicated high-performance threads are explicitly pinned to isolated cores using taskset or pthread_setaffinity

questions.question: What is the purpose of writing to /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches (values 1, 2, and 3), and does it force dirty data to disk?

questions.question: What are Linux POSIX Capabilities, and how do they decompose traditional all-or-nothing root privileges?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

questions.question: What are atomic bitwise operations (such as set_bit and test_and_clear_bit) in operating system kernels, and why are they faster than using mutexes?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

questions.question: What is Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), and how does it protect the operating system against privilege escalation exploits?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: explains that standard ASLR randomizes user-space memory, while KASLR randomizes the base address where the kernel code itself is loaded
explains that historically, the Linux kernel loaded at a fixed physical and virtual address known to all programs
describes how KASLR prevents Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) exploits by making kernel gadget addresses unpredictable
notes that attackers must first find an information leak vulnerability to reveal the randomized offset before exploiting

questions.question: How do storage devices use S.M.A.R.T. monitoring and internal Bad Block Reallocation to hide media degradation from the operating system?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: defines S.M.A.R.T. as self-monitoring analysis and reporting technology embedded in storage drive firmware

describes how firmware detects weak or unreadable sectors and transparently remaps the logical block address to a spare sector
explains that when spare sectors are exhausted, subsequent bad blocks cause unrecoverable I/O errors delivered to the OS

questions.question: What is the difference between changing root directory via chroot and container isolation via Linux namespaces?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: defines chroot as simply changing the apparent root directory ('/') for the current process and its children
explains that chroot does NOT isolate processes, network stacks, IPC, or users (a process inside chroot can still view and kill host processes)

contrasts this with Linux namespaces which provide true multi-dimensional kernel isolation

questions.question: What is the architectural difference between SELinux (Type Enforcement) and AppArmor (Path-Based Enforcement)?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

explains that AppArmor binds security profiles to file path strings (e.g., /usr/sbin/nginx)

contrasts usability: AppArmor is simpler to configure; SELinux provides rigorous Type Enforcement and Multi-Category Security (MCS)

questions.question: How does Network File System version 3 (NFSv3, stateless) differ from NFS version 4 (NFSv4, stateful with file leases)?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: explains that NFSv3 is stateless: every read/write RPC carried full credentials and file handles; server rebooted with zero session state

explains that NFSv4 is stateful: integrates all locking, mounting, and ACLs into a single TCP port (2049)
describes NFSv4 file leases allowing clients to cache file writes locally with server-managed cache invalidation callbacks

questions.question: Why do Linux kernel threads have a small, fixed-size kernel stack (8KB or 16KB), and what occurs if kernel execution overflows it?

questions.question: How does the operating system block layer perform I/O Request Merging (Front-Merging and Back-Merging) to optimize storage throughput?

criteria: explains that adjacent I/O requests directed to contiguous physical sectors can be merged into a single larger I/O command
defines Back-Merging: appending a new block request to the tail of an existing queued request (most common case in sequential writes)
defines Front-Merging: prepending a new block request to the head of an existing queued request
highlights that merging reduces total disk commands, minimizes protocol overhead, and increases DMA transfer sizes

questions.question: How does the VirtIO paravirtualization framework use Split Virtqueues (Descriptor Table, Available Ring, and Used Ring) to transfer data between Guest and Host?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: defines Descriptor Table: stores buffer addresses and lengths in guest physical memory
defines Available Ring: guest driver writes descriptor indices into this ring to notify the host of buffers ready for processing
defines Used Ring: host hypervisor writes processed descriptor indices into this ring to return buffers to the guest
explains that memory-mapped ring buffers allow lockless, high-throughput asynchronous communication between guest and hypervisor

questions.question: How does Energy-Aware Scheduling (EAS) optimize process placement on heterogeneous ARM big.LITTLE / DynamIQ multi-core processors?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: defines big.LITTLE architectures pairing power-efficient 'LITTLE' cores with high-performance 'big' cores

describes the EAS Energy Model calculating energy cost of placing a task on different cores
explains scheduling logic: background or low-utilization tasks are confined to LITTLE cores; heavy compute bursts dynamically migrate to big cores

questions.question: What is the operational difference between Edge-Triggered (EPOLLET) and Level-Triggered (default) modes in Linux epoll?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

questions.question: What is a DMA Bounce Buffer in operating system I/O, and under what hardware limitations is the kernel forced to allocate one?

questions.question: How do UEFI Secure Boot, the Shim loader, and Linux Kernel Lockdown mode combine to guarantee kernel code integrity?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

describes Shim verifying the Linux kernel binary signature before executing it
defines Kernel Lockdown mode: prevents even the root user from modifying running kernel code
identifies restricted operations under lockdown: disables /dev/mem, kexec, raw I/O port writes, and unsigned kernel modules

questions.question: What is the difference between Linux ftrace (function tracing) and kprobes (kernel dynamic probing)?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

contrasts use cases: ftrace traces function execution graphs system-wide; kprobes inspects specific variables and branch conditions

questions.question: How does the O_NOFOLLOW file open flag protect multi-user operating systems against Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) symlink attacks?

questions.question: How do Hazard Pointers solve the Safe Memory Reclamation problem in lock-free concurrent data structures?

defines a hazard pointer as a single-writer, multi-reader global pointer where a thread publishes nodes it is actively reading

describes reclamation: deleting thread scans retired nodes against all active hazard pointers, freeing only unreferenced nodes

questions.question: Why did modern Linux kernels replace classic Ticket Spinlocks with Queued Spinlocks (qspinlock)?

questions.question: How does the pivot_root() system call provide superior container security boundaries compared to chroot()?

questions.question: What is the 'SSD Write Cliff' phenomenon during sustained random write workloads, and how does operating system over-provisioning mitigate it?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

describes the write cliff: once all free blocks are exhausted, every new write forces real-time garbage collection (reading, moving, and erasing blocks)

questions.question: How does the Filter Lock generalize Peterson's two-process algorithm to provide mutual exclusion for N concurrent threads?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

describes the invariant: to enter level L, a thread must pass through level L-1; at least one thread attempting level L is held back
explains the victim variable at each level: the last thread to enter the level is designated the victim and must wait
proves that exactly one thread reaches level N-1 (the critical section), guaranteeing mutual exclusion and progress

questions.question: How do SMB/CIFS Opportunistic Locks (Oplocks) and File Leases allow network clients to cache file data locally while maintaining cluster consistency?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

questions.question: How does Linux Kernel Live Patching (kpatch / livepatch) apply critical security patches to a running kernel without rebooting?

questions.question: What are the three Transparent Huge Page (THP) defragmentation modes ('always', 'madvise', and 'never') in /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag?

questions.question: How does the 'cyclictest' benchmark measure worst-case scheduling latency and jitter in Real-Time Linux operating systems?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: explains that cyclictest sleeps for a precise duration using high-resolution timers (clock_nanosleep) and measures actual wake time
defines latency as the time difference between intended wakeup time and the moment user code actually resumes execution
explains that real-time systems are judged by maximum worst-case latency (tail latency), not average latency
identifies that hardware SMI interrupts, power management state transitions, and kernel spinlocks are primary causes of latency jitter spikes

questions.question: How does Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR) achieve safe memory reclamation in lock-free data structures with lower per-read overhead than Hazard Pointers?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: defines the global epoch counter (e.g., advancing cyclically through epochs 0, 1, 2)
describes reader entry: reading threads announce their active presence by copying the global epoch to a thread-local variable
explains deferred freeing: retired nodes are placed on a per-epoch 'limbo list' and cannot be freed until all threads advance beyond that epoch
highlights the efficiency advantage: readers execute only a single thread-local variable assignment rather than updating hazard pointers on every node dereference

questions.question: How do Packed Virtqueues in VirtIO 1.1 achieve superior CPU cache performance over traditional Split Virtqueues in high-throughput virtualized networks?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: identifies that Split Virtqueues scattered descriptor tables, available rings, and used rings across three disjoint memory regions (poor cache locality)

questions.question: How does the Ceph CRUSH (Controlled Replication Under Scalable Hashing) algorithm calculate data placement in distributed storage without centralized metadata lookups?
questions.subject: Operating Systems

questions.question: How does the Landlock Linux Security Module (LSM) allow completely unprivileged user processes to construct restrictive filesystem sandboxes?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
criteria: explains that traditional security systems (SELinux, seccomp, AppArmor) require root privileges or daemon intervention to configure policies
defines Landlock: an unprivileged user process can create a ruleset and drop all rights except explicit allowed paths via landlock_restrict_self()

questions.question: How does the Linux kernel calculate the 'CommitLimit' under strict overcommit mode (vm.overcommit_memory = 2), and what triggers an allocation failure?

questions.question: How does Linux SMT Core Scheduling prevent cross-hyperthread speculative execution side-channel attacks (such as MDS and PortSmash)?

describes how an isolated task forces sibling hyperthreads to run idle if no matching task exists, eliminating side-channel leakage without disabling Hyper-Threading globally

questions.question: How does the Linux Audit Framework (auditd) use kernel filtering rules and Netlink sockets to achieve tamper-evident event logging with minimal syscall overhead?

questions.question: How do Asymmetric NUMA topologies and Intel Cache Allocation Technology (CAT) prevent 'noisy neighbor' cache thrashing on multi-tenant cloud servers?

questions.question: How do Lock-Free Skip Lists implement concurrent search, insertion, and deletion using atomic Compare-And-Swap (CAS) and logical deletion flags?

questions.question: How does File System Hole Punching (FALLOC_FL_PUNCH_HOLE) allow virtualization hypervisors to dynamically reclaim physical disk blocks when a guest deletes files?

questions.question: What kernel architectural challenges arise during Memory Hotplugging (adding or removing physical RAM from a running operating system without rebooting)?

questions.question: What is the difference between Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) and Immediate Ceiling Priority Protocol (ICPP / Priority Ceiling Emulation)?

questions.question: How do Process-Context Identifiers (PCID) in x86-64 MMUs optimize context switches by eliminating TLB flushes on CR3 register reloads?

questions.question: How does the Linux userfaultfd system call allow user-space applications (like QEMU) to handle page faults for Live Virtual Machine Migration and post-copy memory transfers?

questions.question: In the formally verified seL4 microkernel, how does capability derivation and capability revocation guarantee mathematical proof of access control security?
questions.subject: Operating Systems
